title: 2025-07-29 POC weekly caching sync
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on caching metrics. Reviewed prefix vs KV cache hit rates, prompt reuse patterns, and proposed tuning changes for cache TTLs and normalization. Agreed to run two targeted experiments (aggressive prefix normalization + increased KV cache size) and to share updated benchmark results mid-next-week. Next steps: SE to provide config JSON, customer to share representative prompt traces, schedule in-prod smoke test.
action_items: Maya Liu (Redwood SE) - share suggested cache config (prefix-normalization rules + KV cache sizing) - due 2025-08-01
Carlos Rivera (StratusHealth ML Eng) - export 48h prompt traces and sample request/response pairs (anonymized) - due 2025-07-31
Liam O'Connor (StratusHealth Infra) - provide current VPC egress/firewall rules and KMS key ARN for private pilot - due 2025-08-04
Jordan Patel (Redwood AE) - send updated SOW and pricing options for Dedicated pilot; include burst capacity notes - due 2025-08-01
next_steps: Run two experiments: (1) aggressive prefix normalization + tokenization alignment, (2) increase KV cache allocation and longer TTL for conversational flows
SE to upload config snippets and a short runbook for the experiments
Customer to run experiment in staging and report hit-rate deltas after 48 hours
Schedule 30-min smoke test once config is applied (proposed 2025-08-05)
Jordan to send security docs and pricing
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-29
Time: 10:00am PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Carlos (ML Eng, StratusHealth), Asha (Product), Liam (Infra)

[00:00] Jordan: All right good morning everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check, is this still a good time?
[00:04] Carlos: Yep good for me, thanks.
[00:06] Asha: Morning.
[00:08] Maya: Morning all, Maya on the line.
[00:10] Liam: Liam here.

[00:30] Jordan: Cool. Agenda today is cache hit rates, results from the last week, a couple tuning suggestions from the SE side, and then agree on action items. Maya, do you want to kick us off with the metrics review?

[00:44] Maya: Yeah sure. So we pulled the telemetry from the pilot cluster and looked at two primary things: prefix caching - so the prefix or prompt-level reuse where we can avoid re-computing keys - and KV cache hit rate for multi-turn flows. Quick note, the instrumentation had a small gap Friday night so we patched that, but the bulk of the window is clean.

[01:10] Carlos: When you say prefix caching, is that the same as the prefix/key-value caching we talked about earlier? I always mix up the terms.

[01:16] Maya: Yeah sorry jargon. Prefix cache is like the prefix memoization - when many requests share the same prompt prefix we can reuse the key/value computations. KV cache here means the runtime-level key/value attention cache used across tokens for a single session. They're related but different layers.

[01:32] Asha: Got it. What were the hit rates?

[01:35] Maya: So baseline last week: overall prefix cache hit rate was around 18-22% depending on the route. KV cache hit rate for conversational flows averaged about 55% for short sessions (under 6 turns), but dropped to 28% for longer sessions because of tokenization and prompt variability. We saw 2x improvements on certain templated routes where prompt normalization was applied.

[02:00] Carlos: Hmm 18-22% prefix seems low. We're expecting higher reuse since a lot of requests come from canned templates in the UI. Are you sure the client isn't slightly modifying spacing or metadata that busts the cache?

[02:12] Maya: Exactly, that's one of the findings. In the traces you sent there's a lot of ephemeral metadata inserted into the prompt - user ids, timestamps, microflags - those effectively make the prefix unique. We recommended a normalization pass to strip or canonicalize those fields before hitting the cache.

[02:30] Liam: From infra side, the runtime honors headers but we don't currently rewrite request bodies. If we add normalization at the client or edge layer then we can boost prefix hits without touching the model.

[02:41] Jordan: Would that be a code change for you, Liam? Or can the Redwood SDK do it?

[02:46] Liam: We prefer not to change frontend right now. If Redwood can provide an SDK-side normalizer or a sidecar that runs in the VPC, that'd be ideal.

[03:00] Maya: Totally doable. We have a small normalization library we prototype for customers: trim whitespace, remove ephemeral metadata patterns, canonicalize time formats, and optionally hash or stub large IDs. We can share it as a snippet. Jordan, I'll attach it to the notes.

[03:14] Asha: Will that affect prompt semantics? Some of the metadata is actually used in downstream reranking.

[03:20] Maya: Good point. We recommend a two-tier approach: keep full request payload for model input but compute a normalized prefix tokenization only for caching keys. So the model still gets the metadata in a structured field, but the cache-key normalization strips it.

[03:35] Carlos: OK makes sense. Any numbers on how much normalization helped in your test?

[03:40] Maya: On the templated route we applied normalization in a canary and saw prefix hit rates jump from 21% to 62% and end-to-end token cost drop by ~28% on that route. KV hit rate for multi-turns went from 55% to 71% for short sessions because tokenization aligned more consistently.

[04:02] Carlos: That's promising. The thing I'm worried about is conversation drift; users inject new context. How do you handle TTL and eviction so we don't keep stale prefixes?

[04:12] Maya: We recommend TTLs that map to session semantics. For example, for ephemeral UI-generated prefixes a short TTL like 10-15 minutes; for common system prompts you can justify longer TTLs (hours). Also LRU eviction works well for our access patterns, but for heavy skewed workloads we can do weighted eviction by route.

[04:31] Liam: Any disk/RAM sizing guidance for KV cache? Our clusters are currently sized for nominal loads and we want to avoid OOMs.

[04:38] Maya: For KV cache increase it's more about token volume than query qps. We can provide a sizing matrix: entries per session * average token length. For your pilot traffic we suggested a 1.5x increase in KV memory allocation; that gave about 12-15% higher KV hit rates in our bench. I'll include a config snippet.

[05:00] Jordan: Quick interjection; we ran into a subtle thing on Friday where the telemetry showed 'kay vee cache' events in the logs — and then some of the product names were transcribed oddly. Nothing functional but FYI there's noise in the auto-generated labels.

[05:12] Maya: Heh yeah fireflies transcriptions.

[05:20] Asha: Can you walk through the two experiments again? I want clarity on scope and success metrics.

[05:26] Maya: Sure. Experiment A: aggressive prefix normalization applied at the Redwood edge - strip ephemeral fields, canonicalize formats. Success metrics: prefix hit rate increase >= 30 percentage points on templated routes, and per-token cost reduction >= 20% for those routes after 48 hours. Experiment B: increase KV cache allocation and extend TTL for conversational flows - success metric: KV hit rate increase >= 10 percentage points and p95 latency not to exceed SLA by more than 15%.

[05:58] Carlos: Sounds reasonable. For the normalization, we need to confirm nothing sensitive is exposed. We run HIPAA-sensitive data, so hashing user IDs is mandatory.

[06:10] Maya: Absolutely, hashing/stubbing is part of the snippet. We can also run normalization in your VPC sidecar so raw data never leaves your network.

[06:20] Liam: If the normalizer runs in our VPC, what's the overhead? CPU, latency?

[06:26] Maya: Very small - a few milliseconds per request for typical text sizes. We have microbenchmarks showing <5ms at 99th percentile for 1kB payloads.

[06:34] Asha: Any privacy objections from Redwood side?

[06:37] Jordan: No, running normalizer in customer VPC is fine and aligns with our Private deployment patterns. We'll include that option in the SOW.

[06:45] Carlos: On the KV increase, did you see any p95 regressions during the bench when you upped memory?

[06:52] Maya: No regressions; actually p95 improved slightly because more requests hit the cache and avoided extra decoder work. But we tagged the bench as synthetic; we want to validate with your real traces.

[07:04] Carlos: OK we'll send 48h traces. Anything special about tokenization? We use a custom pipeline that sometimes splits emojis and punctuation oddly.

[07:14] Maya: Yeah tokenization differences are a common cache-buster. Our normalizer includes a tokenization alignment layer — basically tokenize client-side with the same tokenizer used in the runtime and then compute cache key on token sequences. That reduces semantic mismatches.

[07:27] Liam: That sounds heavier. Will that require model artifacts?

[07:31] Maya: We ship a lightweight tokenizer that mirrors the runtime's tokenization algorithm — it's a small lib, not the whole model.

[07:37] Jordan: Quick check — any security/legal asks outstanding? Carlos you mentioned needing SOC2 artifacts last week.

[07:43] Carlos: Yes please send SOC2 and ISO docs. Also want to confirm KMS integration for key rotation.

[07:49] Jordan: Will do — I'll attach our SOC2 summary and the KMS integration guide.

[07:54] Asha: About competitor risk — we had a brief meeting with ManagedCloudAI. They pitched native request rewriting, but their latency was higher. We might still mention them to procurement.

[08:04] Jordan: Noted. We also showed benchmarks vs Anthropic in the eval sheet; I'll refresh that with these new caching numbers.

[08:12] Maya: Back to experiments: for the staging run we suggest enabling detailed tracing flags for the first 48 hours only. That way we can correlate cache keys to request IDs and safely remove traces after analysis.

[08:26] Carlos: Fine with that as long as traces are redacted and don't include PHI.

[08:31] Maya: Understood. We'll redact PII/PHI before leaving your VPC; we can do an on-prem transform if you prefer.

[08:40] Liam: On the deployment side, we'll need the config as a Kubernetes ConfigMap and a short helm patch.

[08:46] Maya: We'll provide both manifest examples.

[08:49] Jordan: Let's go through the timeline: Maya will send config snippets and normalization library by Friday (2025-08-01). Carlos will export traces by Thu (2025-07-31). We will schedule a smoke test after staging run, aiming for 2025-08-05. Anything else?

[09:04] Carlos: I think that's it. Also can you include estimated cost delta for increasing KV cache? Our finance team wants a rough monthly uplift.

[09:11] Jordan: Yes I'll add options in the SOW - we'll show a 1.5x and 2x memory scenario with approximate cost impacts.

[09:18] Asha: One more question: are there any fallback policies if a normalization mismatch causes lower quality?

[09:24] Maya: Yes, we recommend a canary rollout with automatic fallback: if rerank/quality metric drops beyond threshold we can revert to raw-key mode per-route. We'll include canary instructions.

[09:35] Liam: Does Redwood expose per-route tracing in the console so we can see hit rates in real time?

[09:41] Maya: Yes, per-route dashboards are available — token-level cost, prefix and KV hit rates, and a small tracing pane for example requests. We'll enable your team access.

[09:52] Asha: Great.

[09:55] Jordan: Alright let's do a quick recap of action items. Maya, Carlos, Liam?

[10:00] Maya: I'll send normalization lib, config snippets, and a runbook by 2025-08-01.

[10:05] Carlos: I'll export and share 48-hour traces (anonymized) by 2025-07-31.

[10:09] Liam: I'll share VPC/firewall/KMS details by 2025-08-04 and slot time for the smoke test.

[10:15] Jordan: I'll send SOW, pricing options, and security docs by 2025-08-01.

[10:20] Asha: We'll target the staging run next week and update you after 48hrs.

[10:24] Jordan: Thanks everyone, really productive. We'll follow up in email and I will set the smoke test on the calendar.

[10:29] Carlos: Thanks.

[10:30] Maya: Thanks all.

[END]
